newsitem.title: USA: Ralph Lauren hopes for strong IPO demand.
newsitem.headline: Ralph Lauren hopes for strong IPO demand.

text.p: Designer Ralph Lauren's decision to take his fashion house public in a $600 million initial public offering should bring some sparkle back to the flat market for new issues.
Polo Ralph Lauren Corp.'s strong management team, well-established brand name and financial savvy should keep it off Wall Street's worst-dressed list, analysts say.
"This is the most exciting thing coming down the road in quite a long time," said Peggy Farley, chief executive of Amas Securities. "There's no question this is a terrific company."

But Wall Street has not been particularly kind to newly public design firms. IPOs by Donna Karan International Inc., Guess? Inc. , Mossimo Inc., and Designer Holdings Inc. are largely considered flops, because their stocks are sharply below their IPO prices.

"It's not like what happened with Donna Karan last year," said Allison Malkin, retail analyst at Dillon Read & Co. Inc. "Their expense structure got a little bit out of control ... I have a high degree of confidence that that won't happen here."
Manish Shah, editor of the IPO Maven, said he was impressed because Polo has not succumbed to the lure of easy cash by selling out its brand name and diluting its image.
"They have not allowed licensing to exceed more than 12 percent of their total revenues and they have been careful to make sure earnings grow faster than revenues, which is very smart," Shah said.

Sales at Polo Ralph Lauren topped $1.0 billion in fiscal 1996, according to a regulatory filing, with income from operations growing at a 19.1 percent clip, from $63.2 million in fiscal 1992 to $127.1 million in fiscal 1996.
Lauren launched his first brand, Polo, in 1967 with a collection of men's ties and later moved into menswear. The now-famous logo of a polo player astride a horse appeared in 1971.

The company is seen by Wall Street as having wider appeal than many design houses because it has branched successfully into many other premium consumer products: children's and women's clothing, home products such as towels and bedding, and accessories such as eyeglasses, jewelry, and handbags.

"This is one of the great consumer brands, like Estee Lauder Cos Inc. ) or Coca-Cola Co. ) ... And management isn't so 'fashion-forward' so that they put themselves at risk," Dillon Read's Malkin said.
Gucci Group NV, with a similar powerhouse brand name, has been one of the best-performing retail IPOs, more than tripling its price to about $72 from its IPO price of $22.

The Lauren offering could also benefit from the current penchant in the IPO market for large blue-chip-type companies and its strong underwriting team. The IPO will be led by Goldman Sachs, which owns 28 percent of Ralph Lauren. Morgan Stanley and Merrill Lynch will also underwrite the deal.

The market has been depressed for some time, with the first week of April the slowest week this year, according to MCM CorporateWatch. Only three deals priced, raising $47 million. Last week, nine offerings raised $160 million.
This week, 16 deals are on deck, scheduled to raise about $698 million.
"A lot of them are not likely to come. Last week we had just as many, and a lot were postponed or pushed off," said MCM senior analyst Lee Klaskow.

Farley blamed the IPO market's weakness on a more general malaise: "For the IPO market to be successful, you need a mood of optimism, not just in the market but in general. Now we're facing rate hikes, our country is doing so well that growth is flattening, and the dollar is so high we can't sell our products abroad."
